title: Comparing Boxed Integers Without ==
statement:
`==` on two `Integer`s compares *references*, not values -- `Integer` is
a reference type, and `==` never stops meaning "is this the same object"
just because autoboxing makes it easy to forget you are holding one. The
reason this trap is so easy to walk into by accident is that it usually
looks correct: the JLS *requires* `Integer.valueOf` to cache and reuse
objects for every value from `-128` to `127`, so `==` on two boxed
integers in that range genuinely does return `true` when the values are
equal -- right up until a value outside that range breaks the pattern.

## Your function

```
public static int countEqualPairs(List<Integer> values);
```

Return how many pairs of indices `(i, j)` with `i < j` have
`values.get(i)` and `values.get(j)` equal *in value* -- not necessarily
the same object. `values` may be empty or contain values well outside the
`-128`..`127` range.

## Watch out

- **`values.get(i) == values.get(j)` compiles, runs, and passes every
  test built only from small numbers.** Two `Integer`s both holding `5`
  are, by the JLS's own caching guarantee, guaranteed to be the exact
  same cached object -- so `==` happens to agree with `.equals()` for
  every value in `-128..127`. Two `Integer`s both holding `1000` are
  *not* guaranteed to be the same object (autoboxing is free to create a
  new one each time, and typically does outside the cached range), so
  `==` on them is false even though the values are equal.
- **`.equals()` compares values, unconditionally, regardless of range.**
  `values.get(i).equals(values.get(j))` is correct for every input this
  function could ever be given -- there is no range where it needs help
  from anything else.
- **Unboxing before comparing also works, and for the same underlying
  reason.** `values.get(i).intValue() == values.get(j).intValue()`
  compares two primitive `int`s, and primitive `==` has only ever meant
  "equal value" -- the trap is specific to comparing two *references* with
  `==`, not to `==` itself.

generator.source:
"""Random lists of values, always outside the -128..127 Integer cache
range, so a solution comparing with == fails on generated data too, not
just on the fixed tests."""


def generate(rng, count):
    return [_case(rng, i + 1) for i in range(count)]


def _case(rng, index):
    n = rng.randint(0, 12)
    pool = [rng.randint(200, 5000) * rng.choice([1, -1]) for _ in range(4)]
    values = [rng.choice(pool) for _ in range(n)]
    lines = [str(n)] + [str(v) for v in values]
    return {"name": "%d values outside the Integer cache range #%d"
                    % (n, index),
            "stdin": " ".join(lines) + "\n"}

tests.name: an empty list has no pairs
a duplicate within the cached range -- == would happen to work here
a duplicate outside the cached range -- == fails here
tests.description: 1000 is well outside -128..127. Two boxed Integers holding 1000 are not guaranteed to be the same object, so == on them is typically false even though the values are equal.

tests.name: three equal large values -- every pair among them counts
a negative duplicate outside the cached range
duplicates both inside and outside the cached range together
tests.description: 100 is cached (a == solution gets this pair right by luck); 200 is not (a == solution gets this pair wrong).
